body.text: Nvidia founder and long-time CEO Jensen Huang admitted to infidelity on November 8, writing: “I take full responsibility.” He left his position as Nvidia CEO on November 12. Although Huang didn’t mention his affair partner by name, Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter and internal correspondence, reported that Huang had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le.

According to media reports, U.S. intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang acted on behalf of Chinese intelligence. Beijing denied that allegation, which Reuters could not independently verify. Alice Huang has yet to comment publicly on the alleged affair or the espionage accusations.

When Jensen Huang admitted to infidelity, it sparked a firestorm of discussion not only in the United States, but in China as well. In both media discussions and social media comments, the espionage angle attracted the most attention. But the story also acted as a magnet for controversial takes on gender dynamics, particularly in the workplace. (Note that these examples come from one Knews thread and one separate post, not a survey of Chinese opinion.)

Some commenters treated Jensen Huang’s infidelity as an understandable consequence of wealth. In a comment beneath a Knews post about Huang’s extramarital affairs, a reader suggested Jensen Huang probably loved his wife but was surrounded by “各种美食” (“all kinds of delicacies”). The metaphor presented women as temptations and made his conduct sound like an inevitable response to what was on offer.
Another commenter called adultery “standard fare for successful people.”

“Multiple women?” one user asked. Another wrote, “For someone of Jensen Huang’s stature, he wouldn’t count as a scumbag unless he’d been with at least 100 women.” The comment had received 42 likes when captured.
There was pushback, too. Many expressed sympathy for Jensen Huang’s wife. When one user argued that love fades, another replied: “If love fades, then get divorced.”

In the discussion of Alice Huang, meanwhile, sexual speculation also extended to the professional lives of women writ large. Alice Huang had a business career before the scandal. According to Reuters’ review of financial records and corporate materials, she had a career in banking, working for HSBC and then CITIC. She then held a senior position at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management before taking her role as Megaspeed International’s controlling shareholder. Reuters reported that Nvidia listed the Singapore-based cloud-computing company as an official cloud partner in its directory.

One social media user shared what was presented as Alice Huang’s profile, in a post tellingly titled “黄大佬的女人pyq” (roughly, “Big Boss Huang’s woman’s WeChat Moments”). Attractive women, the post claimed, gravitate toward whichever industry is booming – in their professional careers as well in their love lives.

By listing employment alongside dating, the author implied that a woman’s choice of career was simply part of her search for a partner. The post offered no evidence for this assertion, and did not claim any personal knowledge of Alice Huang.

The assumption that women in the workplace are looking for a sexual partner extends far beyond Alice Huang as a individual. Sexual harassment in the workplace is a recurring issue in China. Despite tightened laws, finding justice through the courts is an uphill battle – and often leads to the victim being counter-sued by the alleged harasser.

Sexualized abuse of women extends outside their workplaces. Qingdao Porsche salesperson Mu Qianwen has received media acclaim for her high sales totals. That apparently made her a target for harassment.

Mu contacted police in February 2025 over fabricated sexual material. A man was circulating falsified chat records combining Mu’s promotional images with unrelated explicit videos. One such video received over 9 million views, according to Jimu News. Mu described harassment following the material’s circulation, and said she had even contemplated suicide.
The man had been sentenced to 10 days’ administrative detention and a fine in October 2025. Mu filed a civil complaint on July 27, 2026, seeking clarification and an apology.
